A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: V3 reports original experiments on bias–reasoning correlations, question removal, bias injection, attention patterns, and overthinking mitigation, with additional results in its appendices.

after.justification: V4 retains those original results and adds attention-based early exit, latent-representation diagnostics, MATH500 attention analysis, and measurements of bias during reasoning.

M1.justification: V4 introduces Attn-Exit in Appendix I.3, a distinct inference procedure absent from v3. It checks normalized question attention from layer 21 at sentence boundaries and forces a final answer when attention exceeds a 95th-percentile threshold. The existing question-removal and bias-injection procedures remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Appendix G adds MATH500 for layer-wise attention analysis, extending mathematical dataset coverage beyond the retained AIME benchmarks. The other new diagnostics and Attn-Exit experiment use the existing CharCount (zh) task; the original datasets and language coverage remain.

E2.justification: Table 4 adds Remove to the AIME 2024 comparison alongside Qwen-14B and FCS_SFT. V3 evaluated question removal separately in Table 2 but omitted it from this comparison. The CharCount comparator set, including FCS_SFT, FCS_DPO, SEAL, and PROBE, is retained.

E3.justification: New diagnostic experiments introduce substantial evaluation designs: Appendix J uses a 2,000-example training set and 200-example test set for bias prediction, and five 100-example groups for logit-lens analysis with explicit-output exclusions. Appendix K samples reflection and intervening positions and tests sentence-wise answer probabilities on 100 selected cases. These are new protocols, not revisions to the retained benchmark settings.

E4.justification: Appendix J adds probing and logit-lens analyses testing whether direct answers correspond to latent representations before and during reasoning. Appendix K newly examines attention and bias across reasoning steps, including a high-bias subset. Appendix G also extends the attention analysis to MATH500. These substantially expand validation of the proposed mechanism.

E5.justification: The descriptive standard deviations in v3 Appendix J are retained in v4 Appendix L, with unchanged values, and existing attention error bars are preserved. No new repeated-run counts, seed information, confidence intervals, or significance-testing procedures are reported. Simplifying the bias-injection standard-deviation table changes presentation only.

E6.justification: V4 adds substantial results: Attn-Exit achieves 72.9% accuracy, low/high-deviation lengths of 472.1/516.6 tokens, and RΔ of 9.4% in Table 8; Figure 16 reports probe accuracies reaching 85% and over 72%. Figures 15 and 17–19 add attention, logit-lens, and temporal findings. Table 4 newly reports AIME Remove subgroup lengths of 7252.6/8159.6 and RΔ of 12.5%; its 66.7% accuracy already appeared in v3 Table 2. Existing matched results are retained.

T1.justification: The original bias-distance, length-reduction, and normalized-attention definitions remain unchanged. Appendix J.2 and Figure 17 introduce Δr, a mean-centered statistic derived from normalized counts of internal number-token decoding probabilities exceeding 0.1. This is a limited mathematical-definition addition; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and principal conclusion retain the same claims: internal bias triggers overthinking, question attention can reactivate it, and existing mitigation methods leave its influence. The new diagnostics and preliminary mitigation direction support or extend discussion of these claims without redefining the principal contributions.

C2.justification: The expanded Section 8 discusses possible origins in training and inaccurate knowledge, proposes gradual weakening of bias through declining question attention, and advocates inference-time mitigation. It newly acknowledges that bias remains undefined for open-ended tasks. Appendix I.3 identifies unresolved layer and threshold selection, while Appendix K distinguishes rapid changes in average answer readouts from slower changes in high-bias cases.

D1.justification: V4 adds substantial implementation information for the new analyses: the bias probe’s 5120-input/256-hidden/5-output architecture, layer 24 extraction, mean pooling, KL loss, and learning rate of 1e-5. It also specifies Attn-Exit’s layer and threshold, logit-lens token mappings and exclusions, and the sentence-wise interruption prompt. Existing decoding and fine-tuning details are retained.

R1.justification: Section 2 is substantially expanded into training-time, inference-time, and prompting approaches, with new positioning against chain-of-thought unfaithfulness research, including Turpin et al., Chen et al. (2025c), and Arcuschin et al. V4 distinguishes bias affecting correct reasoning at reflection points from post-hoc rationalization. The bibliography adds numerous works and removes the Wang et al. (2025) and Zhu–Griffiths references.

P1.justification: Editing is concentrated in the rewritten related-work section, the expansion of Conclusion into Conclusion and Discussion, and terminology and appendix-heading adjustments. The acknowledgement is removed. Most existing experimental prose and the main section sequence are preserved, so the revision is not a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: V4 adds Figures 15–19 covering mathematical attention, probe learning curves, logit-lens results, and reasoning dynamics, plus Table 8, which redisplays existing comparators alongside Attn-Exit. Table 4 gains a row, and the bias-injection standard-deviation table consolidates its columns. The original Figures 1–14 retain their graphics; displays are reflowed and conference headers added.

improvement.justification: Appendix J provides useful empirical corroboration for the direct-answer proxy that v3 used without latent-representation validation. Appendix K and the expanded discussion improve the account of bias dynamics and explicitly identify applicability limits. These strengthen the paper, but the new validation remains concentrated on one model and CharCount, does not establish lossless bias measurement, and leaves Attn-Exit’s tuning and robustness unresolved. The evidence supports a limited net quality improvement.
